title: Women's ordination
hookLine: the debate over full ordination for women, told from both sides with respect

lines: A RULE KEPT AS LAID DOWN.
cards: Here's an odd thing about today's argument. Two people who disagree sharply can open the same text, the long account of the Buddha's final months, and each find a line for their side.

One reads a warning about changing rules. The other reads the Buddha naming who belongs in his community. The question: can women be fully ordained as nuns, bhikkhunis, in traditions where that line was lost?
Today both sides speak, each at its best.

teach.h: ONE SIDE: KEEP RULES AS LAID DOWN.
teach.b: The Vinaya says the order of nuns began with Mahapajapati. Lines of fully ordained nuns continue in Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese communities, and those nuns are part of daily temple life.
In Theravada lands the line broke, and Tibetan communities have had no unbroken line of their own. The first side, at its best.
Early in that long discourse, the Buddha tells his monks they can expect to prosper as long as they don't lay down rules never laid down, or throw out rules that were.
The Vinaya says a nun is ordained by a sangha of nuns and then by a sangha of monks.
For monks who hold this view, if the nuns' sangha is gone, no one now has the standing to make a new one, and a way around the rule is just what that discourse warns against.
Keeping the form whole is how they keep faith with the Buddha. The second side, at its best.
Later in the same discourse, Mara urges the Buddha to pass away, and the Buddha says he won't go until his monks, his nuns, and his lay men and women have learned the teaching.

teach.h: THE OTHER: NUNS AMONG FOUR ASSEMBLIES.
teach.b: To supporters of restoring the order, that names four assemblies, nuns among them, as the shape of his community.
Some Theravada women have received full ordination with nuns from East Asian lines taking part, and some monks have stood with them.

teach.h: BOTH POINT TO THE BUDDHA'S WORDS.
teach.b: Both sides are trying to be faithful, and both point to the Buddha's own words.

teach.h: NAME THE DIFFERENCE, NOT A QUARREL.
teach.b: The canon even has a talk for this, the Kinti Sutta: when monks disagree about meaning, go to them gently, show exactly where the difference lies, and don't let it become a quarrel.

how: Fully ordained nuns live and teach in East Asian Buddhist communities; in Theravada and Tibetan communities, women practice as novices, as precept-holding nuns, or in newer bhikkhuni communities, and the question is discussed by monks, nuns and lay people.

o: whether women can again be fully ordained as nuns
whether women may become lay followers
whether nuns may teach lay people in temples

games.q: told with respect: tap the pairs.
p: keep the rules as they were laid down
monks, nuns, lay men and lay women

s: both sides of the debate point to the Buddha's own words
one cites the warning against changing rules; the other, the four assemblies with nuns among them.
those against restoring the line simply dislike women
they argue that the Vinaya's rules for ordination can't be remade once the line is broken.
the Kinti Sutta says to settle a disagreement by out-arguing the other side
it advises showing gently where the difference lies, so it doesn't become a quarrel.

games.q: monks in your community disagree about what a teaching means. what does the Kinti Sutta advise?
o: vote, and ask the losing side to leave
go gently and show exactly where the difference lies
say nothing and let it pass
games.why: the Kinti Sutta advises naming the difference clearly and gently, so it doesn't turn into a quarrel.

practice: Pick a question you feel strongly about, and for a few breaths let your own side speak in your mind, at its best; then let the other side speak as its wisest supporter would, not as a cartoon.
Notice your body tighten or soften, and let both finish their sentences; you don't have to change your mind.

wordCard.voice: Women's ordination. Whether women may again be fully ordained as bhikkhunis where the line was lost, argued by both sides quoting the same teacher. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali parisā: an assembly; the Buddha names four, monks, nuns, lay men and lay women.

carryVoice: Your line: told with respect. Both sides point to the same teacher's words. Until tomorrow.
